extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, and scholars interested in propaganda, media studies, and political communication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for recognizing, producing, and analyzing propaganda across media (news, advertising, social media, education). Covers legal labeling, psychological techniques, channels, and strategic patterns of transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label paid content masquerading as news
rubrics_metrics.description: Any advertisement appearing in the format of a news item must state that the item is in fact a paid advertisement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal law specifically mandates disclosure; paid articles/broadcasts disguised as news are considered 'covert' propaganda because they take on the appearance of objective information rather than propaganda, making the message more easily believed or internalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising as propaganda / uniformity of messaging (branding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising and public relations can be thought of as propaganda that promotes a commercial product or shapes perception of an organization, person, or brand; uniformity of messaging helps define a brand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include commissioned banners, billboards, merchandise (T-shirts, caps) and consistent use of logos/colors/images to create and reinforce a recognizable brand identity (e.g., Hezbollah's post-war merchandising and rallies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Covert propaganda (paid content disguised as news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paid articles or broadcasts presented in the format of news that subjectively and often misleadingly present an issue primarily to persuade rather than inform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These generally use subtle propaganda techniques (not the obvious tactics of traditional ads). Because they mimic objective information, they mislead audiences unless explicitly labeled; regulatory disclosure is required where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biddle's four principles of propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Four principles followed in propaganda: (1) rely on emotions, never argue; (2) cast propaganda into the pattern of 'we' versus an 'enemy'; (3) reach groups as well as individuals; (4) hide the propagandist as much as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles summarize classic propagandistic strategy and can be used as a checklist when evaluating messages for propagandistic intent or design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda model filters shaping news content
rubrics_metrics.description: Five general classes of 'filters' that shape news media content: ownership of the medium; reliance on advertising revenue; access to news sources; threat of litigation and commercial backlash ('flak'); and anti-communism / 'fear ideology'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors regard the first three (ownership, funding, and sourcing) as the most important. The model is intended to explain systemic biases in commercial mass media and can be applied cross-nationally where similar political-economic structures exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasion factors from social psychology and communication theory
rubrics_metrics.description: People can be persuaded by the communicator's credibility, expertise, trustworthiness, and attractiveness; factors like the recipient's degree of interest influence susceptibility via elaboration likelihood and heuristic processing. Humans act as 'cognitive misers' under information overload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these factors to assess why particular messages succeed: when recipients are less motivated or able to process information, superficial cues are more persuasive. Apply elaboration-likelihood and heuristic models to predict message impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bots and automated messages for distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Software agents or bots can populate social media with automated messages and posts of varying sophistication to spread political propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bots were used in the 2016 U.S. election to direct voters to foreign political news sources and to spread politically motivated rumors and false stories; recognize automated patterns, volume, and coordination as indicators of this technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic transmission / indoctrination pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Some propaganda campaigns follow a strategic transmission pattern that begins with a simple transmission (leaflet, advertisement) and includes directions on how to obtain more information, aiming to move the individual from information recipient to information seeker to opinion leader through reinforcement and indoctrination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing campaigns, look for staged calls-to-action, escalation paths to deeper materials, and reinforcement loops designed to convert passive recipients into active disseminators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of social-psychological techniques and logical fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of techniques based in social psychological research are used to generate propaganda; many overlap with logical fallacies because propagandists use arguments that, while sometimes convincing, are not necessarily valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate messages for common fallacies and manipulative psychological appeals (e.g., appeals to fear, authority, in-group bias) as evidence of propagandistic technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting vulnerable audiences (children)
rubrics_metrics.description: Children are especially vulnerable targets for propaganda because they lack critical reasoning and contextual comprehension and are highly imitative; education systems and textbooks can be co-opted for indoctrination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples include Nazi-era curricular materials and picture books; when assessing educational materials or youth-oriented communications, scrutinize simplification, repetition, and moralized slogans that reduce critical engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-propaganda (individual-level persuasion/self-deception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-propaganda refers to an individual convincing themself of something regardless of rational evidence; it functions to lessen cognitive dissonance and is a form of self-deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize internal mechanisms (rationalization, selective attention) that sustain beliefs even without external messaging; consider their role when measuring persistence of propaganda effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda as signaling and intimidation (regime signaling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda may function not primarily to convince but to intimidate the citizenry and signal a regime's strength and ability to maintain control; investment in propaganda can deter challenges by demonstrating capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess resource allocation and visibility of messages as potential demonstrations of power rather than attempts at persuasion; consider signaling effects in authoritarian contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common media channels for transmitting propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Common media include news reports, government reports, historical revision, 'junk science', books, leaflets, movies, radio, television, posters and social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should survey multiple media types and formats; the same message may be adapted across channels to maximize reach and reinforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of data-driven psychological profiling and microtargeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Online human intelligence techniques coupled with psychological profiling using social media data can be used to tailor propaganda messages to individual susceptibilities (e.g., Cambridge Analytica case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence of targeted message variants, illicit data harvesting, and cross-referencing of behavioral data to infer psychological traits; such techniques raise ethical and legal concerns and increase message effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction and overlap between propaganda and disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and to what degree disinformation and propaganda overlap is debated; some define propaganda as use of non-rational arguments to advance or undermine political ideals and disinformation as politically motivated messaging designed to engender public cynicism, uncertainty, apathy, distrust, and paranoia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying messages, consider intent (persuade vs. confuse/undermine), truthfulness (falsehoods vs. emotive framing), and tactics (covert sponsorship, fabrication) rather than relying on a single label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite: identify propagandistic messages before studying transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Information dissemination strategies become propaganda strategies only when coupled with propagandistic messages; identifying these messages is a necessary prerequisite to study the methods by which they are spread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical workflows should begin with content analysis (message framing, claims, appeals) before mapping channels, actors, and diffusion tactics.
